options.text: RNA polymerase synthesizes RNA complementary to a DNA template strand
options.why: RNA polymerase reads one DNA strand and joins complementary RNA nucleotides. Uracil pairs with adenine in the DNA template.

options.text: A ribosome synthesizes mRNA complementary to a DNA coding strand
options.why: Ribosomes translate mRNA into polypeptides. RNA polymerase, rather than a ribosome, produces the RNA transcript.

options.text: RNA polymerase synthesizes DNA complementary to an mRNA template strand
options.why: That describes reverse transcription, which isn't the usual gene-to-protein pathway. D1.2 transcription uses DNA as the template for RNA.

options.text: A ribosome synthesizes a polypeptide complementary to a DNA template strand
options.why: A ribosome uses mRNA, not DNA, during translation. Amino acids also don't form a complementary base sequence.

questions.stem: Why can the same DNA sequence be transcribed repeatedly?

options.text: The DNA bases are copied without being removed, and the separated strands pair again
options.why: Only the hydrogen bonds between the strands are temporarily disrupted. The base sequence and covalent backbones remain intact.

options.text: A replacement DNA strand is synthesized each time the original strand becomes mRNA
options.why: The DNA strand never becomes RNA. Free RNA nucleotides are assembled into a separate complementary transcript.

options.text: RNA polymerase replaces every DNA base immediately after using it in the transcript
options.why: RNA polymerase reads DNA bases without removing them. There aren't missing DNA nucleotides to replace after transcription.

options.text: Both DNA strands stay hydrogen-bonded while RNA polymerase reads through the double helix
options.why: The strands must separate locally so the template bases are exposed. They pair again after the polymerase passes.

questions.stem: Why is transcription a major control point in gene expression?

options.text: Preventing transcription stops production of the gene's RNA and any polypeptide translated from it
options.why: Transcription is the first stage needed to express a protein-coding gene. Controlling it determines whether the RNA message becomes available.

options.text: Preventing transcription changes the gene's DNA sequence so it can no longer be inherited
options.why: Regulating transcription doesn't rewrite the gene. The DNA sequence remains available for later expression and inheritance.

options.text: Preventing transcription blocks replication of that gene while the rest of the genome is copied
options.why: DNA replication copies the genome and is separate from transcription. A gene can be transcriptionally inactive while its DNA still replicates.

options.text: Preventing transcription destroys ribosomes that would otherwise translate every gene in the cell
options.why: Transcriptional control limits particular RNA transcripts. It doesn't destroy the cell's ribosomes or stop every gene being expressed.

questions.stem: Which combination gives the roles of mRNA, tRNA and the ribosome during translation?

options.text: mRNA carries codons, tRNA carries amino acids, and the ribosome catalyzes peptide-bond formation
options.why: These three roles connect a nucleotide sequence to an amino acid sequence. Anticodon pairing places each tRNA's amino acid correctly.

options.text: mRNA carries anticodons, tRNA carries codons, and the ribosome copies the DNA template
options.why: The codons are on mRNA and the anticodons are on tRNA. Copying DNA into RNA is transcription by RNA polymerase.

options.text: mRNA carries amino acids, tRNA forms peptide bonds, and the ribosome supplies the codon sequence
options.why: tRNA carries amino acids, while the mRNA supplies codons. The ribosome holds the components and catalyzes peptide-bond formation.

options.text: mRNA forms the ribosome, tRNA copies the gene, and DNA delivers amino acids for assembly
options.why: Ribosomes contain rRNA and protein, but mRNA acts as the translated message. Neither tRNA nor DNA performs the stated roles.

questions.stem: What does it mean that the genetic code is degenerate?

options.text: More than one codon can specify the same amino acid
options.why: Most amino acids have several codons. This is why some base substitutions don't alter the amino acid sequence.

options.text: One codon can specify several amino acids in the same cell
options.why: That would make the code ambiguous. A codon specifies one amino acid or a stop signal in a given genetic code.

options.text: Codons change their meaning whenever a different protein is translated
options.why: Codon meanings remain consistent across genes. Different proteins result from different codon sequences, not changing definitions.

options.text: Every organism uses a completely different set of codon meanings
options.why: That conflicts with the code's near universality. Codon meanings are shared by almost all organisms, with limited exceptions.

questions.stem: An mRNA sequence is 5′-CCU-AUG-GAA-UGG-UAA-AAA-3′. Which peptide is produced?

options.text: Methionine–glutamic acid–tryptophan
options.why: Translation begins at AUG, continues through GAA and UGG, and ends at UAA. Bases outside those signals don't add amino acids.

options.text: Proline–methionine–glutamic acid–tryptophan
options.why: CCU occurs before the AUG start codon, so it isn't translated in this reading frame. Translation begins with methionine.

options.text: Methionine–glutamic acid–tryptophan–lysine
options.why: UAA is a stop codon, so translation ends before AAA can add lysine. A stop codon contributes no amino acid.

options.text: Proline–methionine–glutamic acid–tryptophan–lysine
options.why: This ignores both control signals. CCU lies before the start codon, and AAA lies after the stop codon.

questions.stem: How can a single base substitution leave a polypeptide's amino acid sequence unchanged?

options.text: The altered codon can specify the same amino acid because the code is degenerate
options.why: Several codons can specify the same amino acid. A substitution that creates one of those synonymous codons is silent at the protein level.

options.text: The ribosome repairs every changed codon before translating the mRNA
options.why: Ribosomes read the mRNA presented to them; they don't repair its sequence. Any correction would require a separate repair process.

options.text: The tRNA changes its attached amino acid whenever the mRNA sequence mutates
options.why: A tRNA remains associated with its particular amino acid. A mutation changes which tRNA can pair with the codon.

options.text: The mutation replaces one DNA nucleotide with an identical nucleotide
options.why: Replacing a nucleotide with the same nucleotide wouldn't be a substitution. A silent substitution changes the codon but not its amino acid meaning.

options.text: RNA is synthesized 5′ to 3′, and the ribosome moves along mRNA 5′ to 3′
options.why: RNA polymerase adds nucleotides at the RNA's 3′ end. The ribosome also reads successive mRNA codons toward the 3′ end.

options.text: RNA is synthesized 3′ to 5′, and the ribosome moves along mRNA 5′ to 3′
options.why: The translation direction is accurate, but RNA synthesis isn't. RNA polymerase produces the transcript in the 5′ to 3′ direction.

options.text: RNA is synthesized 5′ to 3′, and the ribosome moves along mRNA 3′ to 5′
options.why: The transcription direction is accurate, but ribosome movement isn't. Translation proceeds along the mRNA toward its 3′ end.

options.text: RNA and its DNA template are both read from 5′ to 3′ during transcription
options.why: The two strands are antiparallel. RNA polymerase reads the DNA template 3′ to 5′ while synthesizing RNA 5′ to 3′.

questions.stem: What is the function of a promoter in transcription?

options.text: It provides a DNA region where transcription factors and RNA polymerase assemble to begin transcription
options.why: The promoter positions the transcription machinery at the gene. Its role comes before synthesis of the RNA transcript.

options.text: It provides an mRNA codon where the initiator tRNA attaches to begin translation
options.why: That describes the AUG start codon on mRNA. A promoter is a DNA sequence involved in transcription.

options.text: It provides a tRNA site where an amino acid attaches before entering the ribosome
options.why: Amino acids attach to tRNAs through enzymes outside the ribosome. A promoter instead helps initiate transcription on DNA.

options.text: It provides a protein sequence that directs a completed polypeptide into the endoplasmic reticulum
options.why: That describes a signal peptide within a polypeptide. A promoter is a non-coding regulatory region of DNA.

questions.stem: Which change occurs during eukaryotic post-transcriptional modification?

options.text: Introns are removed from pre-mRNA and exons are spliced together
options.why: Splicing converts the initial transcript toward mature mRNA. A 5′ cap and 3′ poly-A tail are also added.

options.text: Introns are removed from DNA and the gene's exons are permanently joined
options.why: RNA processing changes the transcript, not the genome. The introns remain present in the cell's DNA.

options.text: Exons are removed from pre-mRNA and introns are translated by ribosomes
options.why: That reverses the usual outcome. Introns are removed, while joined exons remain in mature mRNA.

options.text: A promoter and a start codon are attached to both ends of the transcript
options.why: The promoter stays in DNA, and the start codon is already encoded in the transcript. Processing adds a cap and poly-A tail.

questions.stem: How can one eukaryotic gene produce different polypeptides without a DNA mutation?

options.text: Different combinations of exons can be joined during alternative splicing
options.why: The resulting mature mRNAs have different codon sequences. Their translation therefore produces different polypeptides from the same gene.

options.text: The ribosome can assign a different amino acid meaning to every codon
options.why: Ribosomes don't redefine the genetic code. Different products arise from different exon combinations in the mature mRNA.

options.text: RNA polymerase can reverse the template strand's sequence during each transcription
options.why: RNA polymerase follows complementary base pairing and doesn't rearrange the template. The variation is introduced during RNA splicing.

options.text: Proteasomes can assemble the same amino acids into several unrelated sequences
options.why: Proteasomes break proteins down rather than assembling them. Ribosomes synthesize the polypeptides encoded by alternatively spliced mRNAs.

questions.stem: During elongation, what happens to a tRNA as it passes through the ribosome?

options.text: It enters the A site, shifts to the P site and leaves through the E site
options.why: The A site accepts the charged tRNA, the P site holds the tRNA associated with the growing chain, and the empty tRNA exits through E.

options.text: It enters the P site, shifts to the E site and receives an amino acid in the A site
options.why: A charged tRNA normally enters at A, not P. It has already received its amino acid before reaching the ribosome.

options.text: It enters the E site, copies a codon and leaves through the P site
options.why: E is the exit site, and tRNA doesn't copy codons. Its anticodon pairs temporarily with the existing mRNA codon.

options.text: It remains in the A site while the mRNA and ribosome move away permanently
options.why: Translocation shifts the tRNA through the ribosome. It doesn't remain fixed in the A site after peptide-bond formation.

questions.stem: Which event converts proinsulin into functional insulin?

options.text: Removal of the C-peptide leaves A and B chains linked by disulfide bonds
options.why: Proinsulin has already lost the signal peptide and folded. Removing the connecting C-peptide produces the mature two-chain insulin molecule.

options.text: Addition of a signal peptide joins the A and B chains by peptide bonds
options.why: The signal peptide is removed when preproinsulin becomes proinsulin. It doesn't join the two chains of mature insulin.

options.text: Removal of all disulfide bonds allows the two chains to function separately
options.why: Disulfide bonds hold insulin's A and B chains together and support its functional shape. They aren't all removed.

options.text: Addition of the C-peptide creates the final binding site of mature insulin
options.why: C-peptide is removed during insulin maturation. It isn't part of the final functional insulin molecule.

questions.stem: What is the role of proteasomes in maintaining a cell's proteome?

options.text: They break down damaged or unneeded proteins, enabling amino acids to be recycled
options.why: Cells continually replace proteins as needs and conditions change. Protein degradation makes their amino acids available for later synthesis.

options.text: They translate mature mRNA and join amino acids into replacement polypeptides
options.why: That is the ribosome's role. Proteasomes work in the opposite direction by breaking existing proteins down.

options.text: They remove introns and join exons to produce mature mRNA transcripts
options.why: That is RNA splicing in the nucleus. Proteasomes act on proteins rather than editing RNA transcripts.

options.text: They copy protein sequences into DNA so useful proteins can be inherited
options.why: Cells don't copy amino acid sequences back into inherited DNA this way. Proteasomes degrade proteins and support amino-acid recycling.
